newsitem.title: USA: NYS budget stalls over welfare, rent rises - reports.
newsitem.headline: NYS budget stalls over welfare, rent rises - reports.

text.p: New York State's budget negotiators were unable to resolve a number of issues over the weekend, even though the pact is nearly four months late, local newspapers said on Monday.

Two of the newspapers, the Daily News and the New York Times, attributed the deadlock to another fight over the rules that that govern apartment rents. According to the News, the biggest fight was whether landlords should be able to raise rents by more than 18 percent to 20 percent on vacant apartments.

When lawmakers announced a new rent rule pact on June 16, Gov George Pataki said the base increase was intended to be 20 percent, according to the New York Times. But he said later that the loophole in the law that would allow for bigger rises was an error made by the Assembly Speaker's staff.
Newsday, citing officials close to the talks, said the key impasses involved retooling welfare in the wake of Washington's decision to end its guarantee of aid to the poor.
It explained Assembly Democrats and Pataki were at odds over who is get state aid after federal benefits run out.

Further, the budget negotiators were fighting about a proposal by Pataki to repeal a part of the law that requires using the minimum or the prevailing wage--whichever is higher--to determine how many hours a welfare recipient must work under new workfare programs.
The paper added there was progress in resolving another issue, an impasse over how many prison cells to build, though details were not available.
Newsday added that before talks slowed, all three sides, the Assembly, the Senate and the governor, wanted to give each side something to point to as a victory.

For Pataki, this would be a multi-year property tax cut, for the Senate, a variety of tax cuts, including a reduction in the gross receipts tax on telephone and electric services, and for the Assembly, an array of education initiatives, including a $2 billion bond referendum to pay for building and renovating schools.
